name: Theron Ashgrove
equipment: A whittled figurine of a stone giant child
A bundle of dried herbs for poultices
A leather cord bracelet given by the people of Triboar
features: Fey Ancestry (Half-Elf racial — advantage on saving throws against being charmed, and magic can't put you to sleep)
Favored Enemy: Giants (you have advantage on Wisdom (Survival) checks to track giants and on Intelligence checks to recall information about them; you gain Giant as a bonus language)

Natural Explorer: Mountains (while traveling in mountain terrain for an hour or more: difficult terrain doesn't slow your group, your group can't become lost except by magical means, you remain alert to danger even when engaged in another activity, you can move stealthily at normal pace when alone, you find twice as much food when foraging, and you learn exact number/sizes/direction of creatures you track)
Fighting Style: Archery (you gain a +2 bonus to attack rolls you make with ranged weapons; already included in longbow attack bonus of +8)
Extra Attack (you can attack twice, instead of once, whenever you take the Attack action on your turn)

Primeval Awareness (you can expend one ranger spell slot to sense whether aberrations, celestials, dragons, elementals, fey, fiends, or undead are present within 1 mile, or 6 miles in your favored terrain; does not reveal location or number)

Ranger Archetype: Hunter — Hunter's Prey: Giant Killer (when a Large or larger creature within 5 feet of you hits or misses you with an attack, you can use your reaction to attack that creature immediately after its attack, provided you can see the creature)
Spellcasting (Wisdom-based, knows a fixed number of ranger spells)

Rustic Hospitality (Folk Hero feature — since you come from the ranks of the common folk, you fit in among them with ease; you can find a place to hide, rest, or recuperate among commoners unless you have shown yourself to be a danger; they will shield you from the law or anyone searching for you, though they will not risk their lives for you)

personality.traits: I am uncomfortable with the name 'Giantsbane' and will visibly wince when someone uses it. I prefer to let my actions speak and become awkward and monosyllabic when praised. I whittle small figurines during rests — mostly animals, but lately the figurines have been giants, and I am not sure what that means.
personality.ideals: The world is not divided into monsters and heroes — it is full of creatures trying to survive. Understanding an enemy is not the same as excusing them. If I can find a way to end this conflict without more killing, I will take it, but I will not hesitate to fight if fighting is necessary.
personality.bonds: I found a stone giant child, wounded and crying, in the aftermath of the Battle of Triboar. I nursed it back to health and led it to safety. That act changed something in me — I cannot see giants as simply enemies anymore. I also owe a debt to the people of Triboar, who call me hero despite my protests, and I will not let their faith be misplaced.
personality.flaws: I second-guess myself constantly. I killed giants at Triboar and became a hero for it, but I also saved a giant child and cannot reconcile the two acts. This moral uncertainty makes me hesitate at critical moments — is this giant an enemy or a frightened child? By the time I decide, the opportunity for action has sometimes passed.

appearance: Theron Ashgrove is a lean, weathered man of thirty-two who looks ten years older, the way people do when they have spent most of their life outdoors in harsh conditions. He stands five feet eleven inches, rangy and spare, with the long-limbed build of a distance runner rather than a fighter. His heritage shows in the subtle points of his ears, half-hidden by unkempt dark brown hair that hangs past his collar and is perpetually tangled with twigs, burrs, and occasionally a confused beetle. His eyes are his most striking feature — a clear, pale green, elven in their sharpness, capable of picking out movement at distances that make human archers envious. His skin is tanned to deep bronze, with a scattering of freckles across his nose and cheekbones that would look boyish if not for the thin white scar that runs from his left temple to his jaw, a souvenir from a hill giant's hurled rock at Triboar. His hands are calloused and permanently stained with wood shavings and sap from his whittling habit, and his fingernails are always slightly dirty no matter how recently he has washed. He wears scale mail over a worn green tunic, practical and unadorned, and a heavy cloak of forest-green wool that has been patched so many times it is more patch than original fabric. His longbow — a beautiful weapon of yew and sinew, the one piece of equipment he maintains with obsessive care — rides across his back. A leather cord bracelet, braided and knotted with small wooden beads, circles his left wrist — a gift from the people of Triboar that he wears with obvious discomfort, as though it does not quite fit. In his belt pouch, visible if you look, is a small whittled figurine of a stone giant child, smooth from being handled often.
backstory:
Theron Ashgrove grew up in a small settlement at the base of the Sword Mountains, the son of a human woodcutter and an elven herbalist who had abandoned her people's longevity for love and never once regretted it. It was a quiet childhood — peaceful in the way that mountain communities can be peaceful, where the greatest dangers were avalanches and wolves and the occasional territorial griffon. Theron learned to track before he could read, to shoot before he could write, and to move through mountain terrain with a silence that unnerved his fully human neighbors.

He became a ranger by necessity rather than ambition. The mountains needed someone to patrol the passes, warn of dangers, and guide lost travelers to safety, and Theron — who preferred the company of trees to people and could track a snow hare across bare rock — was the obvious choice. He spent his twenties alone in the peaks, content with his solitude, building a reputation as a reliable guide and a deadly archer without ever seeking either.

The Battle of Triboar changed everything.

Theron was passing through the town when the hill giants attacked — a raiding party of six, with a score of orcs and bugbears as outriders. It was not the first giant attack since the Ordning shattered, but it was the largest Triboar had faced. The town militia was overwhelmed in minutes. Theron, who had been eating breakfast at the inn, grabbed his bow and did what rangers do: he found high ground and started shooting.

He killed three hill giants that day. Three. A single ranger with a longbow and a quiver of arrows, placing each shot with the precision of someone who had spent years hunting creatures that could kill him if they closed the distance. The first giant took an arrow through the eye. The second took two arrows through the throat. The third — the largest, the one leading the charge — took an arrow through the knee that dropped it to all fours, and then a follow-up through the roof of its open, screaming mouth. The militia rallied. The orcs broke. The remaining giants fled.

Triboar called him Giantsbane. Theron hated it immediately.

He tried to leave town quietly. He got as far as the edge of the forest before he heard the crying. It was a sound he had never heard before — deep, resonant, vibrating in his chest — and when he followed it to its source, he found a stone giant child. Perhaps eight feet tall, barely an adolescent by giant reckoning, huddled in a ravine with a broken arm and a face streaked with tears. It had been separated from its wandering parent during the chaos and had been hiding, terrified, for hours.

Every instinct Theron had developed since the Ordning shattered told him to walk away. Giants were the enemy. Giants were destroying settlements, killing people, upending the order of the world. But this was a child — confused, hurt, alone — and Theron could not reconcile the creature weeping in front of him with the raging monsters he had killed that morning.

He splinted the broken arm. He fed the child the last of his rations. He spent two days tracking the child's parent — a stone giant wandering in a fugue state, carving meaningless patterns into cliff faces — and reunited them. The parent looked at Theron with something that might have been gratitude, or might have been confusion, and then picked up its child and walked into the mountains without a word.

Theron went home and spent a week staring at the ceiling. He had killed three giants and saved one, and he could not determine which act defined him. The people of Triboar sent him a braided bracelet and an invitation to a feast in his honor. He put the bracelet on and did not attend the feast.

He has been tracking giant movements since, trying to understand the pattern — why some giants attack and others wander, why stone giants carve and hill giants raid, what the Ordning meant and what its absence means. He speaks Giant now, learned from careful observation and a phrase book he found in a ransacked library. He whittles figurines of the things he sees, and lately the figurines have been giants: stone giants carving, cloud giants drifting, a small stone giant child with a splinted arm. He does not know what side he is on. He suspects the answer is more complicated than sides.
